extracted.intended_audience: legislators, statesmen, educators, and political philosophers concerned with public education and child-rearing policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for a legislator on how to regulate marriage, child-bearing, and the public education upbringing of youth so as to produce healthy bodies, good manners, and a well-ordered state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate timing and partners of marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator ought to consider the parties and their time of life, that they may grow old at the same part of time, and that their bodily powers may not be different; ... the entering into the marriage state, as far as time is concerned, should be regulated by these periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pairings where the man can have children but the woman is too old, or the woman is young enough to produce children but the man too old to be a father; prevent continual discords arising from such mismatches. Suggested ideal ages: woman about eighteen, man about thirty-seven (a little more or less).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate spacing and succession of children
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought not to be too great an interval of time between [children] and their parents; ... neither should the difference in years be too little, as great inconveniences may arise from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent intervals so wide that parents and children cannot mutually benefit (affection/protection), and prevent intervals so small that proper reverence and household economy are disrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit childbearing to when parents are in bodily perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the body continues in perfection ... the children may be equally perfect; but when the parents are past that age it is better they should have no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat roughly the period of bodily perfection as lasting to about fifty years (or a little more); beyond that, discourage further childbearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate season for conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper season of the year should be observed, as many persons do now, and appropriate the winter for this business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislator may prescribe seasons (e.g., winter) for the begetting of children to improve offspring quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow medical and naturalist precepts about bodily fitness for procreation
rubrics_metrics.description: The married couple ought also to regard the precepts of physicians and naturalists, each of whom have treated on these subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should incorporate or heed contemporary medical/naturalist advice on what bodily dispositions are fit for producing healthy children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure moderate bodily habit for parents
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no occasion that any one should have the habit of body of a wrestler to be either a good citizen ... neither should he be infirm or too much dispirited by misfortunes, but between both these. He ought to have a habit of labour, but not of too violent labour; nor should that be confined to one object only ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote moderate, varied physical conditioning appropriate for freemen; avoid extreme specialised training (wrestler) or excessive infirmity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maternal diet, exercise, and mental calm in pregnancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Women with child should also take care that their diet is not too sparing, and that they use sufficient exercise; ... the mind ought to be kept as tranquil as possible; for as plants partake of the nature of the soil, so does the child receive much of the disposition of the mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislate or encourage appropriate maternal nutrition, moderate exercise, and emotional tranquility to influence offspring health and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit bringing up imperfect or maimed infants
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be a law, that nothing imperfect or maimed shall be brought up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate abandonment/not rearing of deformed or maimed newborns (presented as a civic law in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newborn feeding and abstention from wine
rubrics_metrics.description: When a child is born it must be supposed that the strength of its body will depend greatly upon the quality of its food. ... they feed them chiefly with milk, as being best accommodated to their bodies, but without wine, to prevent any distempers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer milk as infant diet; forbid intoxicants (wine) for infants to avoid disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early habituation to environmental conditions and tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also useful to enure them to the cold when they are very little; ... to enure them to the business of war; for which reason it is customary ... to dip their children in rivers when the water is cold; with others to clothe them very slightly ... whatever it is possible to accustom children to, it is best to accustom them to it at first, but to do it by degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accustom children gradually to desired conditions (cold, cloaking, simple dress) and eventual civic tasks; do so gradually and appropriate to age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early years (0–5): avoid formal instruction and heavy labour; encourage healthy play
rubrics_metrics.description: The next age to this continues till the child is five years old; during which time it is best to teach him nothing at all, not even necessary labour, lest it should hinder his growth; but he should be accustomed to use so much motion as not to acquire a lazy habit of body ... His play also ought to be neither illiberal nor too laborious nor lazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For infants up to five, prioritize physical growth and appropriate play (imitative of future tasks); avoid early heavy work or overly intellectual instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play should imitate future civic tasks and be properly regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: Their play also ought to pave the way for their future instruction: for which reason the generality of their play should be imitations of what they are afterwards to do seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design children's games to model civic roles/skills; avoid amusements that are indecent or corrupting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow disputes among boys as physical and moral exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: They too do wrong who forbid by laws the disputes between boys and their quarrels, for they contribute to increase their growth--as they are a sort of exercise to the body: ... the struggles of the heart and the compression of the spirits give strength to those who labour, which happens to boys in their disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not outlaw all boyish quarrels; regulated conflict can serve as exercise and character-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preceptors must supervise companions and manners; exclude slave company
rubrics_metrics.description: The preceptors also ought to have an eye upon their manner of life, and those with whom they converse; and to take care that they are never in the company of slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard children against bad influences and keep them from improper companionship (e.g., slaves), as part of moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home education until seven; banish indecent speech and images
rubrics_metrics.description: At this time and till they are seven years old it is necessary that they should be educated at home. It is also very proper to banish, both from their hearing and sight, everything which is illiberal and the like. ... the magistrates therefore are to take care that there are no statues or pictures of anything of this nature ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local authorities should remove indecent public expressions (statues, pictures, obscene speech) and keep young children at home-educated until ~7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict attendance at adult theatrical forms until appropriate age
rubrics_metrics.description: It should also be illegal for young persons to be present either at iambics or comedies before they are arrived at that age when they are allowed to partake of the pleasures of the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent exposure of young persons to certain dramatic performances until they reach maturity appropriate for communal dining/pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/common education overseen by the state
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident, then, that there should be laws concerning education, and that it should be public. ... each one is a part of the state, and it is the natural duty of each part to regard the good of the whole: and for this the Lacedaemonians may be praised; for they give the greatest attention to education, and make it public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make education a common, public responsibility rather than private, so all citizens are formed for the state's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether education aims at reason or morals and teach necessities vs. excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are doubts ... whether the object of it should be to improve the reason or rectify the morals. ... It is evident that what is necessary ought to be taught to all: but that which is necessary for one is not necessary for all; for there ought to be a distinction between the employment of a freeman and a slave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify educational aims: basic useful skills for all; noble/liberal education appropriate for freemen; omit mean arts that deform body or promote servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit learning arts that are mean or pursued for gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Every work is to be esteemed mean, and every art and every discipline which renders the body, the mind, or the understanding of freemen unfit for the habit and practice of virtue: for which reason all those arts which tend to deform the body are called mean, and all those employments which are exercised for gain;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude arts from the freeman's education when they corrupt physical form, mental freedom, or are mainly for profit; allow certain liberal arts in moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core educational subjects: reading, gymnastics, music, (painting)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four things which it is usual to teach children--reading, gymnastic exercises, and music, to which (in the fourth place) some add painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reading for utility, gymnastics for courage and bodily form, music for noble leisure and formation of manners; painting as judge of fine arts—each with appropriate emphasis and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of education: form the body first, then the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: It is plain that boys should be first put under the care of the different masters of the gymnastic arts, both to form their bodies and teach them their exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially prioritize bodily formation (gymnastics), delaying heavier intellectual labor until the body has developed; allocate stages: home until 7, 7–puberty, puberty–21.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastics: gentle exercises in youth; postpone violent training
rubrics_metrics.description: That gymnastic exercises are useful, and in what manner, is admitted; for during youth it is very proper to go through a course of those which are most gentle, omitting that violent diet and those painful exercises which are prescribed as necessary; that they may not prevent the growth of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mild gymnastic training in childhood; reserve harder training until after a period post-puberty (three years from puberty allocated to other parts of education). Avoid overtraining in youth which impairs later strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education staging around puberty: avoid simultaneous heavy bodily and mental labour
rubrics_metrics.description: When they have allotted three years from the time of puberty to other parts of education, they are then of a proper age to submit to labour and a regulated diet; for it is impossible for the mind and body both to labour at the same time, as they are productive of contrary evils to each other; the labour of the body preventing the progress of the mind, and the mind of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule education so bodily training and intellectual training do not unduly overlap; permit more strenuous bodily regimen only after a prior interval devoted to other education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include music in education to form manners and leisure judgement, but limit form/practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Music ... was made part of education ... because nature requires that we should not only be properly employed, but to be able to enjoy leisure honourably. ... music is one of the most pleasing things ... and there seems to be a certain connection between harmony and rhythm ... the learning of music is particularly adapted to their disposition; for at their time of life they do not willingly attend to anything which is not agreeable; but music is naturally one of the most agreeable things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach music so children can judge and enjoy noble music and so it forms dispositions; view music as forming moral character (different harmonies affect dispositions). But avoid making children expert virtuosi, avoid parts that inflame passions, and prevent music from making citizens effeminate or unfit for war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select harmonies, rhythms, and instruments that shape good character
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry and music there are imitations of manners; ... different harmonies differ from each other so much by nature, that those who hear them are differently affected ... some fix the disposition, others occasion a change in it; some act more violently, others more liberally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose Doric and other morally appropriate harmonies/rhythms that fix noble dispositions; avoid Lydian or Phrygian modes that produce undesirable passions or excessive enthusiasm. Refer to expert writers on particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical music instruction for judging, not virtuoso performance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that children should have some employment which will amuse them ... it is necessary for them to practise, that they may be judges of the art ... but when they are grown older the practical part may be dropped; while they will still continue judges of what is excellent in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children enough practical music to make them discerning listeners; do not train all youth into professional performers—confine advanced instrumental skill to specialists who pursue it as a vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit certain instruments and performances that inflame passions or impair civic speech
rubrics_metrics.description: They should never be taught to play upon the flute, or any other instrument which requires great skill, as the harp or the like, but on such as will make them good judges ... the flute is not a moral instrument, but rather one that will inflame the passions, and is therefore rather to be used when the soul is to be animated ... the player on the flute is prevented from speaking: for which reason our forefathers very properly forbade the use of it to youth and freemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude instruments (e.g., flute, harp, dulcimer) deemed to inflame passions, deform (facially) or prevent civic speech; prefer simpler instruments that cultivate judgement without fostering effeminacy or servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching disputed, virtuoso, or sensational musical pieces to children
rubrics_metrics.description: They should not be employed in those parts of it which are the objects of dispute between the masters in that science; nor should they perform such pieces as are wondered at from the difficulty of their execution ... but let them learn so much of it as to be able to receive proper pleasure from excellent music and rhythms; and not that only which music must make all animals feel, and also slaves and boys, but more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude showy, technically dazzling repertoire from general education; teach repertoire that cultivates correct taste and moral disposition.
